text: The sun has died in the west, what sets must also rise, but first, it must travel the road
no living eye sees. Twelve hours of night, twelve gates, twelve regions of the underworld,
the old ones called the duat. Beneath the world runs a river, and on it sails a bark,
carrying the soul of the sun, ram-headed, traveling light, having left his body behind.
At each gate a serpent waits, know its name, or do not pass. This is the first law down here.
Nothing opens to the one who cannot name it. In the fourth hour there is no water, only desert,
the desert of Socar, where the sun is beyond his own light and steers by voice alone.
So the bark becomes a serpent, a double-headed serpent breathing fire, and slithers through the sand.
There is a lake of burning water, red as blood, ringed by watching baboons. It is destruction to
those who come without the words, and renewal to those who know them. Fire down here is not punishment.
It is a question, and the answer is knowledge. The great serpent apophis drinks the underworld
river dry to strand the sun, but ISIS speaks, and the bark sails on without water. The word spoken
truly carries what the river cannot, and at the deepest hour of night comes the mystery the
priest whispered about. The soul of the sun lies down with the body of Osiris. The living God
rests in the dead God, the dead God rests in the living, and both are made new. Every hour the
dead wake as the light passes over them. For one hour they live again, then they sleep and wait
for his return. This is the secret the duat keeps. It is not a place of punishment. It is a place of
opposites, where the waters of life run through desert sand. Only by going down into the dark does
anything become truly alive, for the dark is where things are remade. There is a hall down here
called the hall of two truths, and in it no one accuses you. You speak your own innocence,
42 denials, each to a judge you must name. I have not stolen, I have not lied, I have not lied,
I have not lied, I have not caused pain, and all the while your own heart sits on the scales,
and it may speak against you. So the old ones carved a scarab and laid it over the heart and prayed,
do not stand against me. On the other pan a single feather, the feather of
truth, of the order that holds the world together. If the heart is light, the dead are called
true a voice, and the scribe writes the verdict, and nothing is decided until it is written down.
In another land they told it differently. There, below, there was no judgment of deeds and no
dawn. All sat in dust, kings ate clay, the dead wore feathers like birds and never saw light,
and their goddess went down through seven gates, and at each gate she gave up a piece of herself,
crown, rod, robe, until she stood naked before the throne of her sister.
To pass she had to surrender everything, even her life. She hung there three days
until small mourners wept with the queen of the dead, and she was let go.
But the law below keeps its accounts. Someone must always stay. The old stories agree on this much.
Nothing comes back up unchanged. Beyond the last gate waits a ferryman who looks behind him.
Be kind to him. That is the last test, and he will row you across lily lake to the field of reeds.
There, the Egypt you loved, perfected. Wheat and barley that never fail. Everyone you ever loved,
even the dog, even the cat, waiting in an eternal springtime. And in the twelfth hour,
the sun is reborn as the scarab, and the waters of the deep lift the bark up into the arms of
the sky. Morning comes, it always comes. Walk gently here. This is the road every soul travels,
every night in miniature, the small deaths, the small rebirths. The duat is not far away.
It is the night side of your own life, and dawn is its promise.
